claim: Oriens-lacunosum/moleculare (O-LM) cells are inhibitory cells in the hippocampus that gate information flow.
source: Oriens-lacunosum/moleculare (O-LM) cells are inhibitory cells in the hippocampus that gate information flow, firing while phase-locked to theta rhythms.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the functional role of O-LM cells.

claim: O-LM cells fire while phase-locked to theta rhythms.
source: Oriens-lacunosum/moleculare (O-LM) cells are inhibitory cells in the hippocampus that gate information flow, firing while phase-locked to theta rhythms.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the firing behavior of O-LM cells.

claim: Models with h-channels in soma and dendrites exhibit preferred spiking recruitment at high theta (4–9 Hz).
source: We find preferred spiking recruitment of models at high (4–9 Hz) or low (2–5 Hz) theta depending on, respectively, the presence or absence of h-channels on their dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on computational modeling results.

claim: Models with h-channels only in soma exhibit preferred spiking recruitment at low theta (2–5 Hz).
source: We find preferred spiking recruitment of models at high (4–9 Hz) or low (2–5 Hz) theta depending on, respectively, the presence or absence of h-channels on their dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on computational modeling results.

claim: Preferred theta ranges depend on slow delayed-rectifier potassium channels.
source: This also depends on slow delayed-rectifier potassium channels, and preferred theta ranges shift when h-channels are potentiated by cyclic AMP.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on computational modeling results.

claim: Preferred theta ranges shift when h-channels are potentiated by cyclic AMP.
source: This also depends on slow delayed-rectifier potassium channels, and preferred theta ranges shift when h-channels are potentiated by cyclic AMP.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on computational modeling results.

claim: O-LM cells can be differentially recruited by frequency-modulated inputs depending on specific channel types and distributions.
source: Our results suggest that O-LM cells can be differentially recruited by frequency-modulated inputs depending on specific channel types and distributions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the modeling results.

claim: Theta rhythms extend from about 4 to 12 Hz during active exploration and REM sleep in the hippocampus.
source: During active exploration and REM sleep, theta rhythms are a prominent activity in the hippocampus, extending from about 4 to 12 Hz (Colgin, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Colgin, 2013.

claim: Two types of theta activity have been described corresponding to high (7–12 Hz) or low (4–7 Hz) frequencies.
source: Two types of theta activity have been previously described, corresponding to high (7–12 Hz) or low (4–7 Hz) frequencies that are, respectively, atropine-resistant (Type 1) or atropine-sensitive (Type 2) (Buzsáki, 2002; Kramis et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002 and Kramis et al., 1975.

claim: High theta (7–12 Hz) is atropine-resistant (Type 1).
source: Two types of theta activity have been previously described, corresponding to high (7–12 Hz) or low (4–7 Hz) frequencies that are, respectively, atropine-resistant (Type 1) or atropine-sensitive (Type 2) (Buzsáki, 2002; Kramis et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002 and Kramis et al., 1975.

claim: Low theta (4–7 Hz) is atropine-sensitive (Type 2).
source: Two types of theta activity have been previously described, corresponding to high (7–12 Hz) or low (4–7 Hz) frequencies that are, respectively, atropine-resistant (Type 1) or atropine-sensitive (Type 2) (Buzsáki, 2002; Kramis et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002 and Kramis et al., 1975.

claim: Social stimuli elicit high theta rhythms.
source: Moreover, recent work indicates that social or fearful stimuli elicit high or low theta rhythms respectively (Tendler and Wagner, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tendler and Wagner, 2015.

claim: Fearful stimuli elicit low theta rhythms.
source: Moreover, recent work indicates that social or fearful stimuli elicit high or low theta rhythms respectively (Tendler and Wagner, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tendler and Wagner, 2015.

claim: Rhythmic activity of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) neurons in the medial septum-diagonal band of Broca (MS-DBB) can entrain the hippocampus at theta.
source: Furthermore, in vivo studies show that rhythmic activity of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) neurons in the medial septum-diagonal band of Broca (MS-DBB) can entrain the hippocampus at theta (Hangya et al., 2009), and that PV+ MS-DBB neurons are known to specifically target interneurons in the hippocampus (Gulyás et al., 1990; Garrett et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hangya et al., 2009, Gulyás et al., 1990, and Garrett et al., 2014.

claim: PV+ MS-DBB neurons specifically target interneurons in the hippocampus.
source: Furthermore, in vivo studies show that rhythmic activity of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) neurons in the medial septum-diagonal band of Broca (MS-DBB) can entrain the hippocampus at theta (Hangya et al., 2009), and that PV+ MS-DBB neurons are known to specifically target interneurons in the hippocampus (Gulyás et al., 1990; Garrett et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gulyás et al., 1990 and Garrett et al., 2014.

claim: O-LM cells fire during the trough of theta rhythms as recorded during local field potentials in the pyramidale layer of the CA1 region of hippocampus.
source: Oriens-lacunosum/moleculare (O-LM) cells, a particular interneuron type, fire during the trough of theta rhythms as recorded during local field potentials in the pyramidale layer of the CA1 region of hippocampus (Klausberger et al., 2003; Varga et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Klausberger et al., 2003 and Varga et al., 2012.

claim: O-LM cells target the distal dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: O-LM cells target the distal dendrites of pyramidal cells and are part of a feedback inhibitory loop that gates information flow in CA1 (Leão et al., 2012; Maccaferri, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Leão et al., 2012 and Maccaferri, 2005.

claim: O-LM cells are part of a feedback inhibitory loop that gates information flow in CA1.
source: O-LM cells target the distal dendrites of pyramidal cells and are part of a feedback inhibitory loop that gates information flow in CA1 (Leão et al., 2012; Maccaferri, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Leão et al., 2012 and Maccaferri, 2005.

claim: O-LM cells express hyperpolarization-activated inward channels (h-channels).
source: Moreover, they are known to express hyperpolarization-activated inward channels (h-channels) (Maccaferri and McBain, 1996) that would allow them to exhibit post-inhibitory rebound spiking, a cellular component of circuit dynamics (Getting, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maccaferri and McBain, 1996.

claim: H-channels allow O-LM cells to exhibit post-inhibitory rebound spiking.
source: Moreover, they are known to express hyperpolarization-activated inward channels (h-channels) (Maccaferri and McBain, 1996) that would allow them to exhibit post-inhibitory rebound spiking, a cellular component of circuit dynamics (Getting, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Maccaferri and McBain, 1996 and Getting, 1989.

claim: Putative O-LM cells exhibit a peak subthreshold membrane oscillation at 5 Hz.
source: Pike et al. (2000) found that putative O-LM cells exhibit a peak subthreshold membrane oscillation at 5 Hz, within the theta range.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pike et al., 2000.

claim: Upon blockade of h-channels, spontaneous 8 Hz firing in O-LM cells in vitro was substantially reduced.
source: Maccaferri and McBain (1996) showed that upon blockade of h-channels, spontaneous 8 Hz firing in O-LM cells in vitro was substantially reduced.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maccaferri and McBain, 1996.

claim: In a more depolarized state, h-channels in O-LM cells are not expected to contribute to subthreshold oscillations at theta.
source: However, further work has shown that in a more depolarized state, h-channels in O-LM cells are not expected to contribute to subthreshold oscillations at theta (Zemankovics et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zemankovics et al., 2010.

claim: When placed in a high-conductance (in vivo-like) state using dynamic clamp, O-LM cells do not function as theta spiking pacemakers.
source: Furthermore, when placed in a high-conductance (in vivo-like) state using dynamic clamp, O-LM cells do not function as theta spiking pacemakers despite exhibiting subthreshold resonance at theta when h-current was enhanced using dynamic clamp (Kispersky et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kispersky et al., 2012.

claim: O-LM cells respond preferentially to 8 Hz theta frequency-timed inputs.
source: On the other hand, O-LM cells in that study did respond preferentially to 8 Hz theta frequency-timed inputs.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Kispersky et al., 2012.

claim: The preferential response to 8 Hz inputs was maintained even when h-channels were blocked.
source: This response was maintained even when h-channels were blocked, and was found to be dependent on afterhyperpolarization dynamics, presumably from outward potassium currents.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Kispersky et al., 2012.

claim: The preferential response to 8 Hz inputs was found to be dependent on afterhyperpolarization dynamics, presumably from outward potassium currents.
source: This response was maintained even when h-channels were blocked, and was found to be dependent on afterhyperpolarization dynamics, presumably from outward potassium currents.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Kispersky et al., 2012.

claim: Non-uniform dendritic densities of h-channels in excitatory pyramidal cells allow for the integration of spatially disparate excitatory inputs on the dendritic tree to arrive synchronously in the soma.
source: For instance, non-uniform dendritic densities of h-channels in excitatory pyramidal cells allow for the integration of spatially disparate excitatory inputs on the dendritic tree to nevertheless arrive synchronously in the soma (Magee and Cook, 2000; Williams and Stuart, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Magee and Cook, 2000 and Williams and Stuart, 2000.

claim: The distribution of h-channels in O-LM cells is unknown.
source: Although the presence of h-channels in O-LM cells is clear, their distribution is unknown, and our original (Saraga et al., 2003) and later (Lawrence et al., 2006b2006b) multi-compartment O-LM cell models focused on somatic h-channel distributions only given the available experimental data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of knowledge regarding h-channel distribution in O-LM cells.

claim: A given cell type can have quite different ion channel conductance densities for the same channel type and robustly maintain cell type-specific output.
source: Further, it is now known that a given cell type can have quite different ion channel conductance densities for the same channel type and robustly maintain cell type-specific output (Marder and Goaillard, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Marder and Goaillard, 2006.

claim: 32 models were selected from a previously developed database of O-LM cell models, with 16 models expressing somatic H and 16 models expressing somatodendritic H distributions.
source: We selected 32 models from our previously developed database of O-LM cell models, with 16 models expressing somatic H and 16 models expressing somatodendritic H distributions (Sekulić et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model selection process.

claim: All models of a particular distribution (somatic or somatodendritic H) had the same maximum conductance density for H.
source: We extracted highly-ranked models from our database such that all models of a particular distribution (somatic or somatodendritic H) had the same maximum conductance density; however, maximum conductance densities of the other channels were different across models (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model selection criteria.

claim: Somatodendritic inhibitory synaptic inputs more effectively entrain O-LM cell spiking than somatic inputs.
source: Somatodendritic inhibitory synaptic inputs more effectively entrain O-LM cell spiking than somatic inputs
evidence: This is a section heading summarizing a key finding.

claim: Power ratios are significantly higher for all tested frequencies and all models with somatodendritic inputs compared to somatic inputs, regardless of the dendritic H distribution in the models.
source: We found significantly higher power ratios for all tested frequencies and all models with somatodendritic inputs compared to somatic inputs, regardless of the dendritic H distribution in the models (Figure 1G).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1G and statistical analysis.

claim: Somatic H models exhibited a peak in spiking resonance at 3 Hz with sharp drop-off at lower and higher frequencies.
source: A complete examination of responses showed that models with somatic H exhibited a peak in spiking resonance at 3 Hz with sharp drop-off at lower and higher frequencies (Figure 2B, left), whereas models with somatodendritic H showed a peak at 4 Hz with a broader response at theta frequencies (power ratio >0.6 at 4–10 Hz, Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Models with somatodendritic H showed a peak at 4 Hz with a broader response at theta frequencies (power ratio >0.6 at 4–10 Hz).
source: A complete examination of responses showed that models with somatic H exhibited a peak in spiking resonance at 3 Hz with sharp drop-off at lower and higher frequencies (Figure 2B, left), whereas models with somatodendritic H showed a peak at 4 Hz with a broader response at theta frequencies (power ratio >0.6 at 4–10 Hz, Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Somatic H models were recruited to fire at a majority of input cycles for 2–5 Hz input.
source: Examination of rotation number for both types of models demonstrated that somatic H models were recruited to fire at a majority of input cycles for 2–5 Hz input (Figure 2B, right) whereas somatodendritic H models fired at a majority of input cycles for 4–9 Hz (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Somatodendritic H models fired at a majority of input cycles for 4–9 Hz.
source: Examination of rotation number for both types of models demonstrated that somatic H models were recruited to fire at a majority of input cycles for 2–5 Hz input (Figure 2B, right) whereas somatodendritic H models fired at a majority of input cycles for 4–9 Hz (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon blockade of H, there was a prominent hyperpolarization of Vm that resulted in no firing of models under any input frequency.
source: We found that upon blockade of H, there was a prominent hyperpolarization of Vm that resulted in no firing of models under any input frequency, or even with no modulation, using our previously tuned synaptic inputs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Blocking H resulted in modest impairment of spiking resonance at a broad range of theta frequencies, with additional reductions in the high theta range for somatodendritic H models.
source: Thus, blocking H resulted in modest impairment of spiking resonance at a broad range of theta frequencies, with additional reductions in the high theta range for somatodendritic H models.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The partitioning of preferred spiking responses of somatic and somatodendritic H models to low and high theta timed inputs, respectively, was preserved despite H block.
source: However, the partitioning of preferred spiking responses of somatic and somatodendritic H models to low and high theta timed inputs, respectively, was preserved despite H block.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Somatic H models exhibited high synchronization (defined as VS >0.8) at 2–5 Hz.
source: Specifically, somatic H models exhibited high synchronization (defined as VS >0.8) at 2–5 Hz whereas models with somatodendritic H were highly synchronized at the higher theta range of 4–9 Hz (Figure 3A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Models with somatodendritic H were highly synchronized at the higher theta range of 4–9 Hz.
source: Specifically, somatic H models exhibited high synchronization (defined as VS >0.8) at 2–5 Hz whereas models with somatodendritic H were highly synchronized at the higher theta range of 4–9 Hz (Figure 3A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With H block, models with somatic H exhibited no significant reduction in synchronization at any input frequency.
source: With H block, models with somatic H exhibited no significant reduction in synchronization at any input frequency (Figure 3B, left) whereas models with somatodendritic H showed a significant decrease in synchronization at 3–15 Hz (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: With H block, models with somatodendritic H showed a significant decrease in synchronization at 3–15 Hz.
source: With H block, models with somatic H exhibited no significant reduction in synchronization at any input frequency (Figure 3B, left) whereas models with somatodendritic H showed a significant decrease in synchronization at 3–15 Hz (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 3 Hz, 5 Hz, and 8 Hz, somatodendritic H models exhibited a phase advance compared to somatic H models.
source: Accordingly, model responses at 3 Hz, 5 Hz, and 8 Hz – a representative sample of preferred frequency ranges for models across both distributions of H – showed that, in all cases, somatodendritic H models exhibited a phase advance compared to somatic H models (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: With 8 Hz modulation, somatodendritic H models fired at 180° relative to release from inhibition.
source: Interestingly, with 8 Hz modulation, somatodendritic H models fired at 180° relative to release from inhibition.
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Somatic H models exhibited a sharp depolarization immediately upon spike termination with input modulation.
source: We found that, with input modulation, somatic H models exhibited a sharp depolarization immediately upon spike termination, whereas somatodendritic H models were held longer at potentials closer to the spike afterhyperpolarization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Somatodendritic H models were held longer at potentials closer to the spike afterhyperpolarization with input modulation.
source: We found that, with input modulation, somatic H models exhibited a sharp depolarization immediately upon spike termination, whereas somatodendritic H models were held longer at potentials closer to the spike afterhyperpolarization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Kdrs takes on an order of magnitude higher conductance density for all somatodendritic H models, compared to somatic H models.
source: Accordingly, the model parameters show that Kdrs takes on an order of magnitude higher conductance density for all somatodendritic H models, compared to somatic H models, whereas KA takes on a comparable range of values both in somatic as well as somatodendritic H models (Table 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: KA takes on a comparable range of values both in somatic as well as somatodendritic H models.
source: Accordingly, the model parameters show that Kdrs takes on an order of magnitude higher conductance density for all somatodendritic H models, compared to somatic H models, whereas KA takes on a comparable range of values both in somatic as well as somatodendritic H models (Table 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Blocking both H and Kdrs led to no overall change in post-spike Vm trajectories for somatic H models.
source: We found that blocking both H and Kdrs led to no overall change in post-spike Vm trajectories for somatic H models, but changed the post-spike Vm trajectories for somatodendritic H models such that they resembled that of somatic H models (Figure 4B, arrow).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Blocking both H and Kdrs changed the post-spike Vm trajectories for somatodendritic H models such that they resembled that of somatic H models.
source: We found that blocking both H and Kdrs led to no overall change in post-spike Vm trajectories for somatic H models, but changed the post-spike Vm trajectories for somatodendritic H models such that they resembled that of somatic H models (Figure 4B, arrow).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Blocking H and KA did not change the post-spike Vm trajectories for either somatic or somatodendritic H models.
source: On the other hand, blocking H and KA did not change the post-spike Vm trajectories for either somatic or somatodendritic H models (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The broad theta spiking resonance peak in somatodendritic H models was completely abolished with H and Kdrs block.
source: We found that, strikingly, the broad theta spiking resonance peak in somatodendritic H models was completely abolished with H and Kdrs block (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The spectral profile of somatodendritic H models with H and Kdrs block resembled that of somatic H models, with a peak power at 2–4 Hz.
source: In fact, the spectral profile of somatodendritic H models with H and Kdrs block resembled that of somatic H models, with a peak power at 2–4 Hz, or the low theta range (Figure 5A, left, compare with Figure 5C, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: The modulation frequencies for which somatodendritic H models could exhibit one spike per input cycle shifted from 4–5 Hz in control to 2–3 Hz with H and Kdrs block.
source: In particular, the modulation frequencies for which somatodendritic H models could exhibit one spike per input cycle (i.e., rotation number of 1) shifted from 4–5 Hz in control to 2–3 Hz with H and Kdrs block, which is the identical range for somatic H models (Figure 5B, left, compare with Figure 5D, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: For both somatic and somatodendritic H models, there was no broad effect of blocking H and KA on either power ratio, or rotation number, except for an increase in 3 Hz and 5 Hz power ratio for somatodendritic H models as well as a small decrease in 3–5 Hz rotation numbers for somatic H models.
source: We then analyzed power ratios and rotation numbers for all models with H and KA blocked and found that, for both somatic and somatodendritic H models, there was no broad effect of blocking H and KA on either power ratio, or rotation number, except for an increase in 3 Hz and 5 Hz power ratio for somatodendritic H models as well as a small decrease in 3–5 Hz rotation numbers for somatic H models (Figure 5A, right; Figure 5B, right; Figure 5C, right; Figure 5D, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: The ability of somatodendritic H models to exhibit a peak in spiking power in the high theta range was unaffected by H and KA block.
source: Crucially, the ability of somatodendritic H models to exhibit a peak in spiking power in the high theta range, i.e., above 5 Hz, was unaffected, unlike with Kdrs block (Figure 5A, right, compare with Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Vector strength in the high theta range was significantly reduced in somatodendritic H models with H and Kdrs block.
source: In particular, vector strength in the high theta range was significantly reduced in somatodendritic H models with H and Kdrs block, to the point where they could not phase-lock well to 5–15 Hz modulated inputs (VS <0.8, Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was significantly higher synchronization at 2 Hz with H and Kdrs block compared to the case of no block.
source: Interestingly, there was significantly higher synchronization at 2 Hz with H and Kdrs block compared to the case of no block, with an overall synchronization profile resembling that of somatic H, with highly synchronized output at 2–4 Hz (VS >0.8, Figure 6A, orange, compare with Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 3B.

claim: For somatic H models, there was no change in vector strength with either H and Kdrs block nor with H and KA block.
source: Finally, for somatic H models, there was no change in vector strength with either H and Kdrs block nor with H and KA block (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: H and Kdrs, but not KA, constitute a core set of conductances that underlie the ability of somatodendritic H models to be entrained precisely at high theta frequencies.
source: These results collectively show that H and Kdrs, but not KA, constitute a core set of conductances that underlie the ability of somatodendritic H models to be entrained precisely at high theta frequencies, and that blocking of these conductances effectively 'transforms' the spiking profiles of somatodendritic H models into that of somatic H models.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Blocking H and Kdrs effectively 'transforms' the spiking profiles of somatodendritic H models into that of somatic H models.
source: These results collectively show that H and Kdrs, but not KA, constitute a core set of conductances that underlie the ability of somatodendritic H models to be entrained precisely at high theta frequencies, and that blocking of these conductances effectively 'transforms' the spiking profiles of somatodendritic H models into that of somatic H models.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: cAMP modulation of H by shifting V1/2 in models by +5 mV, from the control case of –84 mV to –79 mV, was simulated.
source: We chose to simulate cAMP modulation of H by shifting V1/2 in models by +5 mV, from the control case of –84 mV to –79 mV.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: The choice of +5 mV shift falls well within the range of shifts in V1/2 previously reported in recombinant HCN channels with administration of cAMP.
source: The choice of +5 mV falls well within the range of shifts in V1/2 previously reported in recombinant HCN channels with administration of cAMP (Wainger et al., 2001; Baruscotti et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wainger et al., 2001 and Baruscotti et al., 2015.

claim: For somatic H models, the peak spiking resonance shifted from 2–5 Hz in control to 3–5 Hz with cAMP.
source: For the former, the peak shifted from 2–5 Hz in control to 3–5 Hz with cAMP (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For somatodendritic H models, the peak power ratio shifted from 4–12 Hz to 8–10 Hz with cAMP, and spiking power was suppressed for input frequencies outside of this 8–10 Hz range.
source: For somatodendritic H models, on the other hand, not only did the peak power ratio shift from 4–12 Hz to 8–10 Hz, but spiking power was suppressed for input frequencies outside of this 8–10 Hz range (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Somatic H models shifted the frequencies for which they could be recruited for a majority of input cycles from 2–5 Hz to 3–5 Hz with cAMP.
source: Examining the rotation numbers, somatic H models shifted the frequencies for which they could be recruited for a majority of input cycles (rotation number between 0.5 and 1) from 2–5 Hz to 3–5 Hz (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Somatodendritic H models shifted their frequencies under which a spike was evoked for the majority of input cycles from 4–8 Hz to 8–12 Hz with cAMP.
source: On the other hand, somatodendritic H models shifted their frequencies under which a spike was evoked for the majority of input cycles from 4–8 Hz to 8–12 Hz, coinciding with the shifted peak in power ratio (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Somatic H models with cAMP modulation exhibited a shift from 2–5 Hz to 3–5 Hz in input frequencies for which they could be precisely recruited (VS >0.8).
source: A shift from 2–5 Hz to 3–5 Hz was found in somatic H models with cAMP modulation (Figure 8A, left), and a shift from 4–10 Hz to 8–10 Hz was found in somatodendritic H models with cAMP modulation (Figure 8A, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Somatodendritic H models with cAMP modulation exhibited a shift from 4–10 Hz to 8–10 Hz in input frequencies for which they could be precisely recruited (VS >0.8).
source: A shift from 2–5 Hz to 3–5 Hz was found in somatic H models with cAMP modulation (Figure 8A, left), and a shift from 4–10 Hz to 8–10 Hz was found in somatodendritic H models with cAMP modulation (Figure 8A, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Suppression of phase-locking ability to frequencies outside 8–10 Hz was found in somatodendritic H models with cAMP modulation.
source: Suppression of phase-locking ability to frequencies outside 8–10 Hz was also found in somatodendritic H models, mirroring the reduction in spiking power outside this same range (Figure 8A, right).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: With cAMP modulation, models with differing H distributions still exhibited a division of preferred recruitment and firing precision responses into low and high theta.
source: Overall, with cAMP modulation, models with differing H distributions still exhibited a division of preferred recruitment and firing precision responses into low and high theta, similar to that found in the control simulations.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: cAMP modulation confers phase advance of firing in models, and narrowing of H recruitment and precision in the respective low vs high theta ranges depending on H distribution.
source: Therefore, cAMP modulation confers phase advance of firing in models, and narrowing of H recruitment and precision in the respective low vs high theta ranges depending on H distribution, with an additional enhancement in the high theta range for somatodendritic H models at 8–10 Hz.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The presence of dendritic h-channels in O-LM cells may be an important factor in determining their spiking resonance preferences.
source: We predict that the presence of dendritic h-channels in O-LM cells may be an important factor in determining their spiking resonance preferences.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Whether O-LM cells express dendritic h-channels is currently unknown.
source: Whether O-LM cells express dendritic h-channels is currently unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of knowledge.

claim: HCN2 channel expression has been found in the somata of CA1 O-LM cells, but dendritic expression was not specifically examined.
source: Previous work has found HCN2 channel expression in the somata of CA1 O-LM cells, but did not specifically examine dendritic expression (Matt et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matt et al., 2011.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibit a non-uniform dendritic distribution of h-channels, with sixfold larger current densities in distal dendritic regions compared to proximal ones.
source: Dendritic h-channel expression has been demonstrated in other cell types; for instance, CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibit a non-uniform dendritic distribution of h-channels, with sixfold larger current densities in distal dendritic regions compared to proximal ones (Magee, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Magee, 1998.

claim: Disparate distributions of dendritic h-channels can reproduce somatic O-LM cell responses so long as total membrane h-channel conductance is maintained across models.
source: In our previous work, we examined both uniform and non-uniform distributions of dendritic h-channels and found that disparate distributions can nevertheless reproduce somatic O-LM cell responses so long as total membrane h-channel conductance is maintained across models (Sekulić et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sekulić et al., 2015.

claim: Determining dendritic expression of HCN channel subtypes on O-LM cells is needed to shed light on functional properties of O-LM cells.
source: Our present results suggest that determining dendritic expression of HCN channel subtypes on O-LM cells, e.g., through immunohistochemical studies, is needed to shed light on functional properties of O-LM cells.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: O-LM models with somatodendritic h-channels exhibit spiking preference in higher (Type 1-like) theta range whereas models with somatic h-channels fire in the lower (Type 2-like) theta range.
source: Specifically, O-LM models with somatodendritic h-channels exhibit spiking preference in higher (Type 1-like) theta range whereas models with somatic h-channels fire in the lower (Type 2-like) theta range.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the modeling results.

claim: Type 1 theta originates in dorsal hippocampus and has been associated with spatial memory and cognitive function.
source: Type 1 theta originates in dorsal hippocampus and has been associated with spatial memory and cognitive function whereas Type 2 theta seems to be involved in emotional processing and may originate in ventral hippocampus (Strange et al., 2014; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Strange et al., 2014, Ciocchi et al., 2015, and Patel et al., 2012.

claim: Type 2 theta seems to be involved in emotional processing and may originate in ventral hippocampus.
source: Type 1 theta originates in dorsal hippocampus and has been associated with spatial memory and cognitive function whereas Type 2 theta seems to be involved in emotional processing and may originate in ventral hippocampus (Strange et al., 2014; Ciocchi et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Strange et al., 2014, Ciocchi et al., 2015, and Patel et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of ventral O-LM cells was found to promote Type 2 theta oscillations in ventral hippocampus.
source: Furthermore, activation of ventral O-LM cells was found to promote Type 2 theta oscillations in ventral hippocampus (Leão et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leão et al., 2015.

claim: Depending on dendritic distributions of h-channels and co-regulation with the slow-delayed rectifier channel, O-LM cells may be 'tuned' to be Type 1 theta or Type 2 theta spiking resonators.
source: Taken together with our results, these factors suggest that, depending on dendritic distributions of h-channels and co-regulation with the slow-delayed rectifier channel, O-LM cells may be 'tuned' to be Type 1 theta or Type 2 theta spiking resonators, and thus that this system of channels may constitute an intrinsic 'switch' that varies depending on location along the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and cited literature.

claim: This system of channels may constitute an intrinsic 'switch' that varies depending on location along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Taken together with our results, these factors suggest that, depending on dendritic distributions of h-channels and co-regulation with the slow-delayed rectifier channel, O-LM cells may be 'tuned' to be Type 1 theta or Type 2 theta spiking resonators, and thus that this system of channels may constitute an intrinsic 'switch' that varies depending on location along the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and cited literature.

claim: A gradient of HCN1 to HCN2 was observed in pyramidal neurons across the dorsoventral axis in CA1, with higher ratios of HCN1-to-HCN2 in ventral pyramidal neurons and higher HCN2-to-HCN1 in dorsal pyramidal neurons.
source: Additionally, in CA1, a gradient of HCN1 to HCN2 was observed in pyramidal neurons across the dorsoventral axis, with higher ratios of HCN1-to-HCN2 in ventral pyramidal neurons and higher HCN2-to-HCN1 in dorsal pyramidal neurons (Dougherty et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dougherty et al., 2013.

claim: Ventral pyramidal cells are more excitable than dorsal pyramidal cells by virtue of a more depolarized V1/2 of h-channels and a greater h-channel density compared to dorsal pyramidal cells.
source: This resulted in ventral pyramidal cells being more excitable than dorsal pyramidal cells by virtue of a more depolarized V1/2 of h-channels and a greater h-channel density compared to dorsal pyramidal cells.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Dougherty et al., 2013.

claim: A reverse gradient of HCN1-to-HCN2 in dorsal vs. ventral O-LM cells may exist.
source: Interestingly, our work would predict that a reverse gradient of HCN1-to-HCN2 in dorsal vs. ventral O-LM cells exist, given that the models exhibiting high theta spiking preferences – putatively situated in dorsal hippocampus where the high (Type 1) theta is more prominent – exhibited h-channel characteristics resembling the ventral pyramidal neurons that express high HCN1 densities.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and cited literature.

claim: O-LM cells fire at the trough of hippocampal theta frequencies in vivo as measured in the pyramidale layer, a 180˚ phase delay from inhibitory inputs received from the medial septum-diagonal band of Broca.
source: For instance, O-LM cells fire at the trough of hippocampal theta frequencies in vivo (Varga et al., 2012) as measured in the pyramidale layer, a 180˚ phase delay from inhibitory inputs received from the medial septum-diagonal band of Broca, or MS-DBB (Borhegyi et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Varga et al., 2012 and Borhegyi et al., 2004.

claim: Given dendritic synaptic inputs, O-LM cells require somatodendritic h-channel expression to be precisely recruited during the trough of hippocampal theta activity as observed in vivo.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that, given dendritic synaptic inputs, O-LM cells require somatodendritic h-channel expression to be precisely recruited during the trough of hippocampal theta activity as observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results and cited literature.

claim: The O-LM cell models used are based on a database of multi-compartment models that each include nine voltage-gated ionic currents.
source: The O-LM cell models used in this work are based on a database of multi-compartment models that each include nine voltage-gated ionic currents (Sekulić et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model database.

claim: All simulations were performed in the NEURON simulation environment using the CVODE adaptive time step integration method.
source: All of our simulations were performed in the NEURON simulation environment (Hines and Carnevale, 2001; RRID:SCR_005393) using the CVODE adaptive time step integration method.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methods.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory synaptic rates of 500 Hz and 1000 Hz were used for the case of somatic synaptic input.
source: For our present work, we adopted parameter specifics used by Kispersky et al. (2012) and used the same synaptic rates for the case of somatic synaptic input, with one excitatory and one inhibitory process in the soma.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: Both classes of synapses were modelled using a sum of exponentials with τrise = 0.5ms and τdecay = 6.8ms.
source: Both classes of synapses were accordingly modelled using a sum of exponentials with τrise = 0.5ms and τdecay = 6.8ms.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: Synaptic reversal potentials were set to Eexc = 0 mV and Einh = −80 mV.
source: Synaptic reversal potentials were set to Eexc = 0 mV and Einh = −80 mV, as per Kispersky et al. (2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: Modulation simulations consisted of adjusting the inhibitory synaptic rate (1000 Hz) by ±40%.
source: These consisted of adjusting the inhibitory synaptic rate (1000 Hz) by ±40%, with a higher average Poisson rate during 'peak' periods of the modulated frequency and a lower rate during the 'trough' periods (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: The modulated frequency ranges used in the simulations were 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 25, and 30 Hz.
source: The modulated frequency ranges used in the simulations were 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 25, and 30 Hz, with finer granularity in the theta (4–12 Hz) range compared to higher frequencies since previous studies have shown that O-LM cells have preferential spiking below gamma frequencies (Pike et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: The power ratio is the ratio of the PSD at the modulated frequency to the value at 0 Hz.
source: The power spectrum density (PSD) of the binary trains were computed using the pwelch function in MATLAB, and the power ratio, i.e., ratio of the PSD at the modulated frequency to the value at 0 Hz was computed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method.

claim: Rotation number is the average number of spikes per input cycle, across all input cycles in a model simulation.
source: Recruitment of spiking across modulatory phases was also measured using the rotation number, or average number of spikes per input cycle, across all input cycles in a model simulation (Lawrence et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method.

claim: Vector strength (VS) ranges from [0,1] with 1 indicating perfectly synchronized spikes.
source: VS ranges from [0,1] with 1 indicating perfectly synchronized spikes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analysis method.
